title: Covariates and Power
text:
We run some simple simulations to demonstrate the effect of covariates on power.

Example: Binary covariate associated with outcome

mean_response <- expand.grid(treatment = c('placebo', 'active'),
                         gender = c('male', 'female'))
mean_response$mean_response <- ifelse(mean_response$treatment == 'active', 0.75, 0.25)
mean_response$mean_response <- mean_response$mean_response + ifelse(mean_response$gender == 'female', 0.25, 0)
ggplot(mean_response, aes(treatment, mean_response, fill = gender)) + 
  geom_bar(position = 'dodge', stat = 'identity') +
  ggtitle("Assumed mean response pattern")









set.seed(20130514)
nobs <- 120
sim_data <- cbind(mean_response, data.frame(id = 1:nobs))
sim_data$noise <- rnorm(n=nobs)
sim_data$Y <- with(sim_data, mean_response + noise)
t.test(Y~treatment, data = sim_data)

title: GLS, MMRM, and Power
text:
We use the power calculation formula of Lu, Luo and Chen (2008) for Mixed Models of Repeated Measures, which accomodates general missing data patterns. This formula is implemented in the longpower package. We also verify the formula with a simple simulation.



library(longpower)
library(nlme)
library(mvtnorm)
library(parallel)
library(ggplot2)
library(contrast)





gls_sigma <- 2
gls_weights <- c(1, 1.5, 1.75, 2.0)
placebo_mean <- c(0, 0, 0, 0)
active_mean <- c(0, 1, 1.5, 1.8)
retention <- c(1, 0.9, 0.8, 0.7)
# compound symmetric R
R <- matrix(0.5, nrow = 4, ncol = 4)
diag(R) <- 1
N <- 200





power.mmrm(power=0.80, ra = retention, Ra=R, N=N, sigmaa = gls_sigma*gls_weights[4])


     Power for Mixed Model of Repeated Measures (Lu, Luo, & Chen, 2008) 

             n1 = 100
             n2 = 100
     retention1 = 1.0, 0.9, 0.8, 0.7
     retention2 = 1.0, 0.9, 0.8, 0.7
          delta = 1.798283
      sig.level = 0.05
          power = 0.8
    alternative = two.sided

power.t.test(power=0.80, n = N/2*retention[4], sd = gls_sigma*gls_weights[4])


     Two-sample t test power calculation 

              n = 70
          delta = 1.907529
             sd = 4
      sig.level = 0.05
          power = 0.8
    alternative = two.sided

NOTE: n is number in *each* group


The t-test delta is larger, which is expect given the conservative handling of the assumed retention rate. The MMRM makes use of partial informatin from dropouts.

dd0$Time <- as.numeric(dd0$time)
dd0$trt <- ifelse(dd0$id <= N/2, 0, 1)
dd0 <- as.data.frame(model.matrix(~ -1+id+trt*time+Time, data = dd0))
dd0[,'trt:time1'] <- with(dd0, trt*time1)
dd0$Trt <- as.factor(dd0$trt)
dd0$time <- as.factor(dd0$Time)
dd0$Y0[dd0$trt==1] <- as.matrix(subset(dd0, trt==1, c('trt:time1', 'trt:time2', 
  'trt:time3', 'trt:time4'))) %*% active_mean
dd0$Y0[dd0$trt==0] <- as.matrix(subset(dd0, trt==0, c('time1', 'time2', 
  'time3', 'time4'))) %*% placebo_mean

title: Predicting the age of Alzheimer’s symptom onset from a blood test: evaluating a prognostic claim
text:
Philip S. Insel1* and Michael C. Donohue2
1Department of Psychiatry and Behavioral Sciences, University of California, San Francisco, CA, USA
2Epstein Family Alzheimer’s Therapeutic Research Institute, Keck School of Medicine, University of Southern California, San Diego, CA, USA
*Corresponding author: philip.insel@ucsf.edu

title: Predicting the age of Alzheimer’s symptom onset from a blood test: evaluating a prognostic claim
text:
Participants
Participants in the progressor analyses were cognitively unimpaired at their initial clinical visit (CDR 0) and had at least one plasma %p-tau217 measure. The progressor analyses used data shared by the original authors: Knight ADRC and ADNI participants who progressed to symptomatic AD (CDR > 0). The survival analyses used contemporary ADNI data (downloaded 10 July 2026), including nonprogressors, and the common-trajectory analysis used the ADNI clock-development sample (n=345). As in the original report, clock estimation required at least two plasma %p-tau217 values within the range used to develop the clocks, separated by at least one year, and clock assignment required at least one in-range value.10

title: Predicting the age of Alzheimer’s symptom onset from a blood test: evaluating a prognostic claim
text:
Plasma %p-tau217
As in the original report, plasma %p-tau217, the ratio of phosphorylated to non-phosphorylated tau at position 217, was measured by liquid chromatography–mass spectrometry (C2N Diagnostics). The positivity threshold was 4.06, corresponding to an amyloid PET level of 20 centiloids, and the clocks were developed over the range 1.06 to 10.45.10

title: Predicting the age of Alzheimer’s symptom onset from a blood test: evaluating a prognostic claim
text:
Clock estimation
TIRA estimates the time required to pass from one biomarker level to another by integrating the reciprocal of the modeled rate of accumulation.5 For plasma %p-tau217, individual rates were estimated with a linear mixed-effects model and related to the level at the midpoint of follow-up with a generalized additive model.10 SILA samples biomarker versus age data to establish the relationship between rate and level, and integrates it numerically by Euler’s method into a curve of biomarker level against time.4
For the progressor analyses, TIRA and SILA estimates were supplied by the authors of the original report; participants with more than one plasma sample were assigned the average of their estimates.

title: Predicting the age of Alzheimer’s symptom onset from a blood test: evaluating a prognostic claim
text:
Clinical measures
Cognitive status was assessed with the Clinical Dementia Rating (CDR). Symptomatic AD was defined as a CDR global score greater than 0 with a diagnosis of an AD syndrome.10 For the survival analyses, participants were required to be cognitively unimpaired (CDR 0) at the qualifying blood draw. Onset was dated to the start of the interval in which impairment occurred, and it had to persist at the last assessment and occur after the estimated age at positivity. Participants who progressed before their estimated age at positivity, or to a non-AD syndrome, were censored at their last unimpaired assessment. Clinical syndrome was assessed using the CDR by experienced clinicians blinded to biomarker results.10

title: Predicting the age of Alzheimer’s symptom onset from a blood test: evaluating a prognostic claim
text:
Statistical analysis
In each analysis, the aim was to separate the association attributable to biomarker signal from the association produced by two design features: a shared component, in which the same quantity enters both the predictor and the outcome, and a bound, in which the outcome is confined to a region fixed by the predictor.
We decomposed the clock into age at blood draw, defined as age at the first plasma collection, and estimated time from %p-tau217 positivity (time from positivity). In the first set of analyses, age at symptom onset was regressed by ordinary least squares on age at blood draw, on time from positivity, and on the clock-estimated age at positivity, each separately, and the clock was compared with a model using age at blood draw and raw %p-tau217 directly, by adjusted R² and the Akaike information criterion (AIC).15 As a null comparison, time from positivity was replaced with a random value drawn uniformly over the same range, 10,000 times, to generate the distribution of adjusted R² expected from the design constraints alone. In a sensitivity analysis, these comparisons were repeated after excluding participants whose symptom onset preceded the blood draw: the clock is proposed to predict when symptoms will begin in people who are cognitively unimpaired, and for a participant whose blood was drawn after onset, the onset it is used to predict has already occurred.
In the second set, age was removed from the outcome by regressing time from blood draw to symptom onset on time from positivity, estimated by TIRA, by SILA, and as a random value. Because onset was required to follow estimated positivity, a participant not yet positive at the draw could be included only if onset occurred after the time at which the clock places positivity, so time from positivity sets a floor on time to onset. For participants already positive at the draw, the floor falls before the draw and places little constraint on the observed time to onset, so we repeated the analysis restricted to this group. If the association reflects biomarker information, it should persist in this group; if it reflects the bound, it should largely disappear.
In the third set, time from positivity to symptom onset (observed age at onset minus estimated age at positivity) was regressed on estimated age at positivity, estimated in the same three ways. Because the outcome is age at onset minus the predictor, the covariance between them equals the covariance between age at onset and the predictor minus the variance of the predictor, and is negative even when the biomarker carries no information.16
In the fourth set, nonprogressors were included and interval-censored proportional hazards models (icenReg,17 as in the original report) were fit on two timescales: age, as in the original report, and time from the blood draw or from estimated positivity for participants not yet positive at the draw, which excludes immortal time before an event could be counted.18,19 Confidence intervals were obtained by bootstrap resampling (5,000 samples), and individual prediction intervals from the fitted survival curves. Survival curves are shown until fewer than five participants remained under observation.
In the fifth set, we tested the assumption that individuals at the same %p-tau217 level progress at the same rate. In the ADNI clock-development sample (n=345), participant-specific rates of change were estimated from a linear mixed model with random intercepts and slopes and regressed on %p-tau217 level, using either the observed value at the first plasma collection or the model-based value at the midpoint of follow-up, with uncertainty propagated by resampling (2,000 draws from each participant’s conditional distribution of intercept and slope).


Show code: data preparation
# The original authors supplied four files, one per cohort (Knight ADRC, ADNI) and clock method (TIRA, SILA). Each row is a progressor with the following columns:
# 
# | Column | Description |
# |:--|:--|
# | `ID` | Anonymized participant identifier (unique within file only) |
# | `baseline_plasma` | %p-tau217 at the first plasma collection |
# | `baseline_plasma_age` | Age at the first plasma collection (age at blood draw) |
# | `ptau217_positivity_age` | Clock-estimated age at %p-tau217 positivity |
# | `age_of_symptom_onset` | Observed age at symptom onset |
# | `duration` | Supplied interval from positivity to onset (not used; recomputed below) |
# 
# From these we derive the clock's blood-test component, estimated time from positivity, by inverting the clock's definition (age at positivity = age at blood draw − time from positivity), and the other intervals used below. We also add a **random comparator**: for every participant, time from positivity is replaced with a draw from a uniform distribution that respects the same design constraints as the real estimates, namely that positivity precedes onset (lower limit) and the largest SILA estimate observed (upper limit). The random comparator therefore has the same shared age component and the same bound as the clock, but contains no biomarker information.

data_dir <- "Petersen progressor subsets"
if (!dir.exists(data_dir)) {
  stop("The progressor data are not public and are not included in this ",
    "repository. Request them from the authors of Petersen et al. (2026) and ",
    "save the four CSV files in '", data_dir, "/'.")
}

read_progressors <- function(file, source, method) {
  read.csv(file.path(data_dir, file)) %>%
    mutate(Source = source, Method = method)
}

dat <- bind_rows(
  read_progressors("progressors_ADNI_TIRA_anon.csv",  "ADNI",        "TIRA"),
  read_progressors("progressors_ADNI_SILA_anon.csv",  "ADNI",        "SILA"),
  read_progressors("progressors_KADRC_TIRA_anon.csv", "Knight ADRC", "TIRA"),
  read_progressors("progressors_KADRC_SILA_anon.csv", "Knight ADRC", "SILA")) %>%
  mutate(
    # ptau217_positivity_age = baseline_plasma_age - time_from_positivity,
    # so the blood-test component of the clock is:
    time_from_positivity = baseline_plasma_age - ptau217_positivity_age,
    # years from symptom onset to the blood draw (negative = onset after draw)
    time_from_onset = baseline_plasma_age - age_of_symptom_onset,
    # The supplied ID is file-specific, so link the same person across the
    # TIRA and SILA files by cohort, age at blood draw and %p-tau217.
    id = paste(Source, baseline_plasma_age, baseline_plasma) %>%
      as.factor() %>% as.numeric())

if (with(dat, any(duplicated(paste(Method, id))))) {
  stop("Participant keys are not unique within method.")
}

# ---- Random comparator ----
# Upper limit for random time from positivity: the largest SILA estimate.
max_pos <- dat %>%
  filter(Method == "SILA") %>%
  pull(time_from_positivity) %>%
  max()

# The random comparator is built for every participant in either method
# sample. All TIRA participants also appear in the SILA sample except one in
# Knight ADRC (id 53), who is added explicitly. The lower limit,
# time_from_onset, enforces the inclusion rule that estimated positivity must
# precede onset (time from positivity >= draw age - onset age).
set.seed(20260317)
random_time_from_positivity <- dat %>%
  filter(Method == "SILA" | id == 53) %>%
  arrange(Source, Method) %>%
  mutate(
    Method = "Random",
    time_from_positivity = runif(n(), min = time_from_onset, max = max_pos),
    ptau217_positivity_age = baseline_plasma_age - time_from_positivity)

dat <- dat %>%
  bind_rows(random_time_from_positivity) %>%
  mutate(
    Source = factor(Source, c('Knight ADRC', 'ADNI')),
    Method = factor(Method, c('TIRA', 'SILA', 'Random')),
    # outcome of Figure 4: time from estimated positivity to onset

    time_baseline_to_onset = age_of_symptom_onset - baseline_plasma_age)

  pivot_longer(

title: Predicting the age of Alzheimer’s symptom onset from a blood test: evaluating a prognostic claim
text:
Participants
Data provided by the authors comprised participants from the original report who were cognitively unimpaired at their first clinical assessment, developed cognitive impairment with an AD syndrome after estimated %p-tau217 positivity, and remained impaired with an AD syndrome at their last assessment: 59 (TIRA) and 61 (SILA) individuals from the Knight ADRC and 20 (TIRA) and 22 (SILA) from ADNI, described in Supplementary Table 2 of Petersen et al.10 Clinical follow-up began before the first plasma collection, and 11% to 15% of these participants had symptom onset before their blood draw (Knight ADRC: 7 of 61 for SILA and 8 of 59 for TIRA; ADNI: 3 of 22 for SILA and 3 of 20 for TIRA). Median clinical follow-up was 13.0 to 13.2 years in the Knight ADRC progressors (11 assessments) and 10.1 years in the ADNI progressors (10.5 assessments).
The ADNI survival sample comprised 200 participants who were cognitively unimpaired at the qualifying blood draw and had a SILA-estimated age at %p-tau217 positivity. Median age at blood draw was 74.1 years, 54.0% were female, median education was 16 years, 27.5% carried at least one APOE ε4 allele, and median follow-up from blood draw was 8.22 years. Thirty progressed to symptomatic AD after their estimated age at %p-tau217 positivity. Seven progressed before their estimated age at positivity and 30 to a non-AD diagnosis; both groups were censored at their last unimpaired assessment. The remaining 133 were unimpaired at their last assessment and were censored at that time. For the analysis with follow-up starting at the blood draw or estimated positivity, 64 participants whose follow-up ended before their estimated age at positivity were excluded, including the 7 who progressed before positivity, leaving 136 participants and 30 events. In 76 of these, follow-up began at the estimated age at positivity.
The analyses that follow model three outcomes: age at symptom onset, time from blood draw to onset, and time from %p-tau217 positivity to onset. Each analysis in the original report contains a shared component: the same quantity enters both the predictor and the outcome, so the two are correlated by construction. All three analyses are also restricted to individuals whose age at symptom onset was greater than their estimated age at positivity. This inclusion rule bounds the outcome, so it cannot take just any value and is confined to a region fixed by the predictor. The rule is the same for every outcome; only the quantity that sets the bound changes. Either feature alone is sufficient to manufacture an association, whether or not the biomarker carries any information. The shared component and the bound for each outcome are described in the sections that follow.

title: Predicting the age of Alzheimer’s symptom onset from a blood test: evaluating a prognostic claim
section: Age at symptom onset: a shared component and a bound
text:
Age at symptom onset: a shared component and a bound
In the original report, age at symptom onset was regressed on the clock’s estimated age at %p-tau217 positivity, defined as age at blood draw minus estimated time from positivity. Age at blood draw is therefore the shared quantity: it enters the predictor directly, and it is contained in the outcome, since age at onset equals age at blood draw plus time from blood draw to onset.
Age at blood draw also bounds the outcome. Onset could be observed only within a limited window of clinical follow-up, which began before the blood draw, so age at onset is confined to a fixed band around age at blood draw, from 5.7 years before to 16.4 years after blood draw in Knight ADRC (Figure 1).
The original report attributed adjusted R² values of 0.337 to 0.612 to the clock-estimated age at %p-tau217 positivity as a predictor of age at symptom onset.10 When the clock was decomposed into age at blood draw and estimated time from %p-tau217 positivity, the biomarker timing term alone explained essentially no variance in age at symptom onset in either cohort: adjusted R² = 0.02 (TIRA) and 0.01 (SILA) in the Knight ADRC cohort (Figure 1) and adjusted R² = −0.02 (TIRA) and 0.00 (SILA) in ADNI (Supplementary Figure S1). TIRA and SILA estimates in Knight ADRC are shown in Supplementary Figure S2. Age at blood draw alone explained far more: adjusted R² = 0.54 for both method samples in Knight ADRC, and adjusted R² = 0.71 (TIRA sample) and 0.61 (SILA sample) in ADNI.


Show code: statistics for Figure 1 and Supplementary Figures S1-S2
# Full TIRA + SILA + Random versions (Supplementary Figures S1 and S2)
panel_stats_adni  <- compute_panel_stats(dat_long, "ADNI")
panel_stats_kadrc <- compute_panel_stats(dat_long, "Knight ADRC")

# Main-text version (Figure 1): Knight ADRC, TIRA and the random comparator
# only. Re-leveling Method (rather than just filtering rows) drops the unused
# "SILA" level so facet_grid() does not draw an empty row.
drop_sila <- function(df) {
  df %>%
    filter(Method != "SILA") %>%
    mutate(Method = factor(Method, levels = c("TIRA", "Random")))
}
dat_tira      <- drop_sila(dat)
dat_long_tira <- drop_sila(dat_long)

panel_stats_kadrc_tira <- compute_panel_stats(dat_long_tira, "Knight ADRC")

Show code: Figure 1
plot_panels(dat_long_tira, "Knight ADRC", panel_stats_kadrc_tira,
  seg_data_kadrc_tira, constraint_kadrc_tira, y_pos_override = 120)








Figure 1: Relationships in Knight ADRC between the predicted outcome (age at symptom onset) and three predictors: age at blood draw (first plasma collection), estimated time from %p-tau217 positivity, and their difference, age at blood draw minus estimated time from %p-tau217 positivity (ie, estimated age at %p-tau217 positivity). Time from %p-tau217 positivity is estimated by the TIRA method (top row) or by randomly sampling from a uniform distribution over the observed range of estimates (bottom row); results for the SILA method are shown in Supplementary Figure S2. Panels include fitted linear regression estimates, summary statistics for each predictor, and a dashed identity line. To illustrate the contribution of time from %p-tau217 positivity (middle column), the rightmost panels show faint grey lines connecting each person’s age at blood draw to their estimated age at %p-tau217 positivity. The pink regions span the observed window of onset, from 5.7 years before to 16.4 years after the blood draw. Because onset was observed only within this window, the data are constrained to a fixed band around the identity line, and age at blood draw determines age at onset up to that interval.





Incorporating the biomarker timing term through the clock produced some improvement over age alone in Knight ADRC (adjusted R² = 0.60–0.61 vs 0.54; ΔR² = 0.06–0.07). However, this improvement was largely driven by participants whose blood was drawn after symptom onset (7 of 61 for SILA; 8 of 59 for TIRA). These draws came from people who were already cognitively impaired, whereas the analysis is premised on predicting time to symptoms in people who are cognitively unimpaired (CDR 0); for these participants, the clock recovers an onset that has already occurred rather than predicting one. When they were excluded, the clock’s advantage over age fell to less than 0.02 for both methods (SILA: adjusted R² = 0.55 for the clock vs 0.54 for age; TIRA: 0.56 for the clock vs 0.55 for age). In ADNI the clock performed worse than age alone (TIRA: adjusted R² = 0.34 for the clock vs 0.71 for age; SILA: 0.47 for the clock vs 0.61 for age) and worse than a random comparator (adjusted R² = 0.56, Supplementary Figure S1), and excluding participants with onset before the draw (3 in each sample) widened the gap (TIRA: 0.33 for the clock vs 0.83 for age; SILA: 0.47 for the clock vs 0.74 for age).


Show code: excluding participants with onset before the blood draw
# Repeat the Figure 3 model comparison without participants whose symptom
# onset preceded the blood draw (time_baseline_to_onset < 0). These
# participants were already impaired when blood was drawn, so the clock
# "predicts" an onset that had already occurred. Produces the adjusted R2
# values quoted in the text for this sensitivity analysis.
sensitivity <- bind_rows(
  `All progressors` = fit_model_comparison(dat),
  `Onset after blood draw` = fit_model_comparison(
    dat %>% filter(time_baseline_to_onset >= 0)),
  .id = "Sample") %>%
  select(Sample, Source, Method, N, Model, Adj_R2) %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = Model, values_from = Adj_R2)


Under the design-constrained null, in which biomarker timing information was replaced by random values, the nominal Type I error rate of the clock was severely inflated. In Knight ADRC, 100% of simulated analyses produced statistically significant associations (p<0.05), despite the absence of biomarker information; in ADNI, 98.5% were significant. The median null adjusted R² ranged from 0.43 to 0.49, accounting for most of the observed predictive performance: 77 to 82% of the observed adjusted R² in the Knight ADRC analyses and 91 to 141% (greater than 100% indicates worse performance than the median null value) of the observed adjusted R² in ADNI. Thus, the magnitude of the reported associations is largely what would be expected from the study design alone, even when biomarker information is removed, and in the case of ADNI, worse than expected.


Show code: design-constrained null simulation
# Produces the null results quoted above: Type I error (share of null fits
# with p < 0.05), the median null adjusted R2, and the median null as a
# percentage of the observed adjusted R2 (`null_summary`).

# For one cohort x method sample, repeatedly replace time from positivity
# with a random draw that respects the design constraints (positivity
# precedes onset; upper limit max_pos), rebuild age at positivity, and refit
# the original report's regression of age at onset on age at positivity.
make_null_r2 <- function(df, n_iter = 1000) {
  map_dfr(seq_len(n_iter), function(iter) {
    df_null <- df %>%
      mutate(
        rand_time = runif(n(), min = time_from_onset, max = max_pos),
        rand_ptau_age = baseline_plasma_age - rand_time)

    fit <- summary(lm(age_of_symptom_onset ~ rand_ptau_age, data = df_null))

    tibble(
      iter = iter,
      adj_r2 = fit$adj.r.squared,
      r2 = fit$r.squared,
      `p-value` = fit$coefficients["rand_ptau_age", "Pr(>|t|)"])
  })
}

# 10,000 null replicates per sample. This takes a few minutes, so the result
# is saved to disk (not version controlled) and reused on later renders.
null_file <- "null-dist.rdata"
if (file.exists(null_file)) {
  load(null_file)
} else {
  set.seed(20260910)
  null_dist <- expand_grid(
    Source = c("ADNI", "Knight ADRC"),
    Method = c("SILA", "TIRA")) %>%
    mutate(
      data = map2(Source, Method,
        \(src, meth) dat %>% filter(Source == src, Method == meth)),
      null = map(data, make_null_r2, n_iter = 10000)) %>%
    select(-data) %>%
    unnest(null)
  save(null_dist, file = null_file)
}

null_dist <- null_dist %>%
  mutate(Source = factor(Source, c("Knight ADRC", "ADNI")))

# Observed adjusted R2 for the clock (the original report's analysis)
obs_r2 <- dat %>%
  filter(Method %in% c("SILA", "TIRA")) %>%
  group_by(Source, Method) %>%
  summarise(
    obs_adj_r2 = summary(lm(age_of_symptom_onset ~ ptau217_positivity_age))$adj.r.squared,
    .groups = "drop") %>%
  mutate(Method = as.character(Method))

# Null quantiles, Type I error (share of null fits with p < 0.05), and the
# percentile of the observed value within the null distribution
null_summary <- null_dist %>%
  left_join(obs_r2, by = c("Source", "Method")) %>%
  group_by(Source, Method) %>%
  summarise(
    obs_adj_r2 = first(obs_adj_r2),
    null_lo = quantile(adj_r2, 0.025),
    null_median = median(adj_r2),
    null_hi = quantile(adj_r2, 0.975),
    percentile = mean(adj_r2 <= obs_adj_r2),
    `Type I error` = mean(`p-value` < 0.05) * 100,
    .groups = "drop") %>%
  mutate(p_empirical = 2 * pmin(percentile, 1 - percentile))

title: Predicting the age of Alzheimer’s symptom onset from a blood test: evaluating a prognostic claim
section: Time from blood draw to symptom onset
text:
Time from blood draw to symptom onset
Removing age at blood draw from the outcome, by modeling time from blood draw to symptom onset rather than age at onset, removes the shared quantity but not the bound. The bound now comes from estimated time from %p-tau217 positivity, because the inclusion rule requires the time of onset to exceed the time of positivity. A participant with a time from positivity of −5 years, predicted to become positive 5 years after the blood draw, could be included only if onset occurred more than 5 years after the draw. For every participant not yet positive at the draw, time from positivity therefore sets a floor on time to onset. We show this by regressing time from blood draw to symptom onset on time from positivity, a regression in which age at blood draw appears on neither side. Participants not yet positive at the draw are pushed into the upper left of Figure 2, and a negative slope is guaranteed whether or not the biomarker carries any information.
In Knight ADRC, time from positivity explained a substantial share of the variance in time to onset in the full sample, where the bound constrains participants not yet positive at the draw (adjusted R² 0.28 to 0.31), and a random comparator performed similarly (0.26). When the analysis was restricted to participants already positive at the blood draw, for whom the bound falls before the draw and has little effect, adjusted R² fell to 0.01 to 0.03 (Figure 2). In ADNI, adjusted R² was negative in the restricted sample for both methods (Supplementary Figure S3).


Show code: helpers for Figure 2 and Supplementary Figure S3
# Statistics for Figure 2 / S3: regression of time from blood draw to onset
# (y) on time from positivity (x), in all participants and restricted to
# those already positive at the draw (x >= 0).
time_to_onset_stats <- function(df, ...) {
  df %>%
    mutate(x = time_from_positivity, y = time_baseline_to_onset) %>%
    group_by(...) %>%
    summarise(
      N = sum(complete.cases(x, y)),
      rho = cor(x, y, method = "spearman", use = "complete.obs"),
      fit = list(lm(y ~ x)),
      fit_pos = list(lm(y ~ x, subset = x >= 0)),
      .groups = "drop") %>%
    mutate(
      beta = map_dbl(fit, ~ coef(.x)[2]),
      alpha = map_dbl(fit, ~ coef(.x)[1]),
      adjR2 = map_dbl(fit, ~ summary(.x)$adj.r.squared),
      adjR2_pos = map_dbl(fit_pos, ~ summary(.x)$adj.r.squared),
      label = stats_label(beta, alpha, adjR2, rho, N, adj_r2_extra = adjR2_pos),
      # labels sit in the lower left, below the bound where there are no data
      x_pos = -15,
      y_pos = -20)
}

# The bound as a pink wedge: positivity must precede onset, so
# time to onset >= -(time from positivity), i.e. the region above y = -x. The
# upper edge is the largest observed time to onset. The wedge is identical in
# every panel (it is fixed by the design, not fit to each panel's data).
make_wedge <- function(df) {
  x_rng <- range(df$time_from_positivity, na.rm = TRUE)
  y_max <- max(df$time_baseline_to_onset, na.rm = TRUE)
  tibble(x = seq(x_rng[1], x_rng[2], length.out = 200)) %>%
    mutate(
      y_min = pmin(-x, y_max),   # capped so the wedge tapers to a point
      y_max = y_max)
}

plot_time_to_onset <- function(df, stats, wedge) {
  ggplot(df, aes(x = time_from_positivity, y = time_baseline_to_onset)) +
    geom_point(size = 2.5, alpha = 0.4) +
    # all participants
    geom_smooth(method = 'lm') +
    geom_ribbon(data = wedge, aes(x = x, ymin = y_min, ymax = y_max),
      inherit.aes = FALSE, alpha = 0.25, fill = "pink") +
    # restricted to participants already positive at the draw; its adjusted
    # R2 appears in parentheses in the label, in the same color
    geom_smooth(
      data = df %>% filter(time_from_positivity >= 0),
      method = 'lm', se = FALSE, linetype = "solid", color = "darkred") +
    geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "grey40") +
    geom_richtext(
      data = stats,
      aes(x = x_pos, y = y_pos, label = label),
      hjust = 0, vjust = 0, lineheight = 1.1, size = 3.5,
      fill = NA, label.color = NA, show.legend = FALSE) +
    ylab("Time from blood draw to symptom onset (yrs)") +
    xlab("Estimated time from %p-tau217 positivity (yrs)") +
    theme_jama() +
    theme(strip.text = element_text(size = 15)) +
    coord_cartesian(xlim = range(df$time_from_positivity))
}

Negative values of estimated time from positivity indicate participants not yet positive at the blood draw (left of the dashed vertical line). The pink region shows the values permitted by the design: because onset must follow estimated positivity, time to onset cannot fall below the diagonal. Blue lines show linear fits in all participants, with 95% confidence bands; dark red lines show fits restricted to participants already positive at the blood draw. Each panel reports the regression equation, adjusted R² for all participants (restricted sample in parentheses), Spearman ρ, and N.

title: Predicting the age of Alzheimer’s symptom onset from a blood test: evaluating a prognostic claim
text:
Direct use of %p-tau217
When %p-tau217 was entered into the model directly, as a raw level alongside age at blood draw, it outperformed the clock in every cohort and for every clock method (Figure 3). In ADNI, however, raw %p-tau217 added little beyond age at blood draw alone. Excluding participants whose blood was drawn after symptom onset widened the advantage of age and raw %p-tau217 over the clock in Knight ADRC: adjusted R² was 0.67 for age and raw %p-tau217 vs 0.55 for the clock (SILA) and 0.67 for age and raw %p-tau217 vs 0.56 for the clock (TIRA).

Figure 3: Model comparison across cohorts and clock methods. Adjusted R² for four models of age at symptom onset in Knight ADRC (top row) and ADNI (bottom row): age at blood draw alone (dark), the clock-derived age at %p-tau217 positivity (orange in the SILA column, blue in the TIRA column), a random comparator for age at %p-tau217 positivity from a single draw uniformly over the observed range (grey), and age at blood draw together with raw %p-tau217 level (red). title: Predicting the age of Alzheimer’s symptom onset from a blood test: evaluating a prognostic claim
section: Relocation of the bound: time from %p-tau217 positivity to symptom onset
text:
Relocation of the bound: time from %p-tau217 positivity to symptom onset
The original report also regressed time from %p-tau217 positivity to symptom onset on estimated age at positivity. Here the shared quantity is the predictor itself: the outcome is age at onset minus estimated age at positivity, so the predictor enters the outcome with a negative sign, and the two are negatively correlated by construction. Estimated age at positivity also bounds the outcome. Because observed symptom onset in these cohorts falls between roughly 68 and 98 years, the duration can be at most 8 years for someone positive at 90 and must be at least 8 years for someone positive at 60 (shaded regions, Figure 4; TIRA, SILA and both cohorts are shown in Supplementary Figure S4). The reported finding that older age at positivity is associated with a shorter time to symptom onset therefore follows from the design, independent of any biomarker signal. Replacing the clock-derived estimate with age at blood draw minus a randomly generated time reproduced a negative association of similar magnitude to the SILA and TIRA estimates.


Show code: helpers for Figure 4 and Supplementary Figure S4
# Statistics for Figure 4 / S4: regression of time from positivity to onset
# (y) on estimated age at positivity (x). Labels sit near the top of each
# panel (y = 45).
duration_stats <- function(df, ...) {
  df %>%
    mutate(x = ptau217_positivity_age, y = time_from_positivity_to_onset) %>%
    group_by(...) %>%
    summarise(
      N = sum(complete.cases(x, y)),
      rho = cor(x, y, method = "spearman", use = "complete.obs"),
      fit = list(lm(y ~ x)),
      x_min = min(x, na.rm = TRUE),
      x_max = max(x, na.rm = TRUE),
      .groups = "drop") %>%
    mutate(
      beta = map_dbl(fit, ~ coef(.x)[2]),
      alpha = map_dbl(fit, ~ coef(.x)[1]),
      adjR2 = map_dbl(fit, ~ summary(.x)$adj.r.squared),
      label = stats_label(beta, alpha, adjR2, rho, N),
      x_pos = x_max - 0.7 * (x_max - x_min),
      y_pos = 45)
}

# The bound as a pink band: within a cohort, onset was observed only between
# ages a_min and a_max, so for estimated age at positivity x the duration
# (onset age - x) must lie in [a_min - x, a_max - x]. Computed per cohort.
make_onset_band <- function(df, ...) {
  df %>%
    group_by(...) %>%
    summarise(
      x_lo = round(min(ptau217_positivity_age)),
      x_hi = round(max(ptau217_positivity_age)),
      onset_lo = round(min(age_of_symptom_onset)),
      onset_hi = round(max(age_of_symptom_onset)),
      .groups = "drop") %>%
    mutate(x = map2(x_lo, x_hi, seq)) %>%
    unnest(x) %>%
    mutate(y_min = onset_lo - x, y_max = onset_hi - x)
}

plot_duration <- function(df, stats, band) {
  ggplot(df, aes(x = ptau217_positivity_age, y = time_from_positivity_to_onset)) +
    geom_point(size = 2.5, alpha = 0.4) +
    geom_smooth(method = 'lm') +
    geom_richtext(
      data = stats,
      aes(x = x_pos, y = y_pos, label = label),
      hjust = 0, vjust = 1, lineheight = 1.1, size = 3.5,
      fill = NA, label.color = NA, show.legend = FALSE) +
    geom_ribbon(data = band, aes(x = x, ymin = y_min, ymax = y_max),
      inherit.aes = FALSE, alpha = 0.3, fill = "pink") +
    ylab("Time from positivity to symptom onset (yrs)") +
    xlab("Estimated age at plasma %p-tau217 positivity (yrs)") +
    theme_jama() +
    theme(strip.text = element_text(size = 15))
}

title: Predicting the age of Alzheimer’s symptom onset from a blood test: evaluating a prognostic claim
section: Survival models on two timescales: age at symptom onset vs time to symptom onset
text:
Survival models on two timescales: age at symptom onset vs time to symptom onset
Including nonprogressors, as in a survival analysis, might be expected to resolve these problems, since the sample is no longer restricted to those who progressed. On the age timescale used in the original report, however, the shared quantity remains: age at blood draw enters both the predictor, estimated age at positivity, and the outcome, age at symptom onset. The bound also remains, because onset is counted as an event only when it occurs after estimated age at positivity. In the ADNI survival sample (n=200; 30 events), a survival analysis with the shared quantity found estimated age at positivity was associated with symptom onset on the age timescale (HR 0.87, 95% CI 0.81 to 0.95, P<0.001; Figure 5, panel a).
We then measured time to symptom onset from the blood draw, or from the estimated time of positivity for participants not yet positive at the draw. This removes the shared quantity, because age no longer appears in the outcome; it removes the bound, because no follow-up precedes estimated positivity; and it removes immortal time bias,18,19 because follow-up before the blood draw and before estimated positivity, when no event could be counted, is no longer included. On this timescale, estimated age at positivity was not associated with symptom onset (n=136; 30 events; HR 1.02, 95% CI 0.96 to 1.09, P=0.51; Figure 5, panel b). The predictor and events are identical in the two analyses.
No participant’s 95% prediction interval for time to onset reached an upper limit within follow-up (Figure 5, panel c): the model cannot say when, or whether, any individual will develop symptoms.


Show code: ADNI data (ADNIMERGE2)
# Figures 5 and 6 use ADNI data from the ADNIMERGE2 R package, which ADNI
# distributes to approved data users (https://adni.loni.usc.edu). The analysis
# code was written by PSI; only the data loading below is specific to
# ADNIMERGE2.
library(ADNIMERGE2)
library(silaR)     # SILA clock (https://github.com/Betthauser-Neuro-Lab/silaR)
library(icenReg)   # interval-censored proportional hazards models
library(lme4)      # linear mixed model for Figure 6
library(mgcv)      # GAMs for Figure 6
library(qgam)      # quantile GAMs for the Figure 6 prediction band
library(patchwork) # multi-panel figures

PTAU_LO  <- 1.06   # lower bound of %p-tau217 range used for clock development
PTAU_HI  <- 10.45  # upper bound
PTAU_POS <- 4.06   # positivity threshold (SILA val0)
SILA_DT  <- 0.25   # SILA integration step (years)
MIN_SPAN <- 1      # minimum years (rounded to 0.1) between first and last draw
                   # for clock development

# The preprint used ADNI clinical data downloaded on 10 July 2026. ADNIMERGE2
# is updated as visits are added, so clinical records dated after that are
# dropped to reproduce the published sample exactly.
DATA_CUTOFF <- as.Date("2026-07-10")

# Plasma %p-tau217 (C2N PrecivityAD2, FNIH Biomarker Consortium samples)
c2n_ptau217 <- FNIHBC_BLOOD_BIOMARKER_TRAJECTORIES %>%
  filter(PLASMA_BIOMARKER == "C2N_plasma_ptau217_ratio") %>%
  transmute(RID, ptau_date = as.Date(EXAMDATE),
    ptau217 = suppressWarnings(as.numeric(TESTVALUE))) %>%
  filter(!is.na(ptau217))

# Date of birth is recorded as month/year; use the 15th of the month
demog <- PTDEMOG %>%
  filter(!is.na(PTDOB)) %>%
  distinct(RID, .keep_all = TRUE) %>%
  transmute(RID, dob = as.Date(paste0("15/", PTDOB), "%d/%m/%Y"),
    PTGENDER, PTEDUCAT)

# APOE genotype as e33, e34, ...
apoe <- ADSL %>%
  transmute(RID = as.numeric(SUBJID), apoe = paste0("e", gsub("[^0-9]", "", APOE)))

# Diagnosis etiology: "AD" if MCI or dementia is due to Alzheimer's disease
dx <- DXSUM %>%
  filter(as.Date(EXAMDATE) <= DATA_CUTOFF) %>%
  transmute(RID, VISCODE2,
    DXMDUE = case_when(DXMDUE == "MCI due to Alzheimer's Disease" ~ "AD",
                       !is.na(DXMDUE) ~ "Other"),
    DXDDUE = case_when(DXDDUE == "Dementia due to Alzheimer's Disease" ~ "AD",
                       !is.na(DXDDUE) ~ "Other")) %>%
  distinct(RID, VISCODE2, .keep_all = TRUE)

# CDR global and box scores (ADNI codes missing as negative values)
cdr_secondary <- c("CDORIENT", "CDJUDGE", "CDCOMMUN", "CDHOME", "CDCARE")
cdr <- CDR %>%
  filter(!is.na(VISDATE), VISDATE <= DATA_CUTOFF) %>%
  mutate(across(c(CDGLOBAL, CDMEMORY, all_of(cdr_secondary)),
    ~ replace(.x, .x < 0, NA))) %>%
  distinct(RID, VISCODE2, .keep_all = TRUE)

# One row per CDR visit. CDGLOBAL is missing at some visits where box scores
# were recorded; global CDR > 0 iff memory >= 0.5 or >= 2 secondary boxes
# >= 0.5 (Washington University scoring rules), so impairment is recoverable.
adni_visits <- cdr %>%
  select(RID, VISCODE2, cdr_date = VISDATE, CDGLOBAL, CDMEMORY,
    all_of(cdr_secondary)) %>%
  left_join(dx, by = c("RID", "VISCODE2")) %>%
  inner_join(demog, by = "RID") %>%
  left_join(apoe, by = "RID") %>%
  mutate(cdr_impaired = if_else(
    !is.na(CDGLOBAL), CDGLOBAL > 0,
    CDMEMORY >= 0.5 | rowSums(across(all_of(cdr_secondary)) >= 0.5) >= 2))

# In-range %p-tau217 values, with years since each participant's first one
ptau_long <- c2n_ptau217 %>%
  filter(ptau217 > PTAU_LO, ptau217 < PTAU_HI) %>%
  group_by(RID) %>%
  mutate(v0_date = min(ptau_date),
    ptau_years = round(as.numeric(ptau_date - v0_date) / 365.25, 2)) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  arrange(RID, ptau_years) %>%
  inner_join(demog %>% select(RID, dob), by = "RID") %>%
  mutate(age = round(as.numeric(ptau_date - dob) / 365.25, 2))

# Clock development: >= 2 in-range values spanning >= 1 year (n = 345).
# Clock assignment: >= 1 in-range value.
draw_span <- ptau_long %>%
  group_by(RID) %>%
  summarize(n_draws = n(), span = round(max(ptau_years), 1))
clock_dev_ids    <- draw_span$RID[draw_span$n_draws >= 2 & draw_span$span >= MIN_SPAN]
clock_assign_ids <- draw_span$RID




Show code: SILA clock and survival data
# ---- SILA clock: estimated age at %p-tau217 positivity ----
res <- sila(
  ptau_long %>% filter(RID %in% clock_dev_ids) %>%
    select(subid = RID, age, val = ptau217),
  dt = SILA_DT, val0 = PTAU_POS, maxi = 200)

# Each participant is placed on the curve by their first in-range value
sila_est <- sila_estimate(res$tsila,
    ptau_long %>% filter(RID %in% clock_assign_ids) %>%
      select(subid = RID, age, val = ptau217),
    align_event = "first") %>%
  filter(age == ageref) %>%
  select(RID = subid, est_age_pos = estaget0)

# Origin = first in-range blood draw; one row per CDR visit on or after it
ptau_base <- ptau_long %>%
  group_by(RID) %>%
  slice_min(age, n = 1) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  select(RID, v0_date, age_v0 = age) %>%
  inner_join(sila_est, by = "RID")

visits_ptau <- adni_visits %>%
  inner_join(ptau_base, by = "RID") %>%
  filter(cdr_date >= v0_date) %>%
  mutate(cdr_age     = round(as.numeric(cdr_date - dob) / 365.25, 1),
         age_v0      = round(age_v0, 1),
         est_age_pos = round(est_age_pos, 1)) %>%
  filter(cdr_age >= age_v0 - 0.01)

# ---- Onset definition and interval-censored survival data ----
sm <- function(x) if (length(x)) max(x) else NA_real_
sn <- function(x) if (length(x)) min(x) else NA_real_

surv_base <- visits_ptau %>%
  filter(!is.na(cdr_impaired)) %>%
  arrange(RID, cdr_age) %>%
  mutate(imp    = cdr_impaired,
         imp_ad = imp & coalesce(DXMDUE, DXDDUE) %in% "AD") %>%
  group_by(RID) %>%
  summarize(
    origin_age = first(age_v0), est_age_pos = first(est_age_pos),
    sex = first(PTGENDER), edu = first(PTEDUCAT), apoe = first(apoe),
    cu_at_origin = !first(imp), n_visits = n(), last_age = max(cdr_age),
    imp_at_last = last(imp),
    # onset = start of the FINAL impaired-AD run; NA unless the last visit
    # is impaired-AD, so persistence to the last assessment is enforced
    .lastbad  = sm(cdr_age[!imp_ad]),
    onset_age = sn(cdr_age[imp_ad & cdr_age > coalesce(.lastbad, -Inf)]),
    # last cognitively unimpaired assessment before onset
    pre_onset_age = sm(cdr_age[!imp & cdr_age < coalesce(onset_age, -Inf)]),
    first_imp_age = sn(cdr_age[imp]),
    last_cu_age   = sm(cdr_age[!imp & cdr_age < coalesce(first_imp_age, Inf)]),
    .groups = "drop") %>%
  # cognitively unimpaired at the qualifying blood draw, with follow-up
  filter(cu_at_origin, n_visits >= 2) %>%
  mutate(
    ad_onset = !is.na(onset_age),
    bio_neg  = ad_onset & onset_age <= est_age_pos,   # onset before positivity
    event    = ad_onset & !bio_neg,
    # non-AD syndrome, or AD syndrome with onset preceding estimated
    # positivity: censored at the last cognitively unimpaired assessment
    cens_imp = bio_neg | (!ad_onset & !is.na(first_imp_age) & imp_at_last),
    # interval for onset, in years from the blood draw (R = Inf if censored)
    L = pmax(case_when(event    ~ pre_onset_age - origin_age,
                       cens_imp ~ coalesce(last_cu_age, origin_age) - origin_age,
                       TRUE     ~ last_age - origin_age), 0),
    R = if_else(event, onset_age - origin_age, Inf),
    L_age = origin_age + L,
    R_age = origin_age + R)

# Timescale (b): at-risk time starts at the later of the blood draw and the
# estimated age at positivity; participants whose follow-up ended before
# estimated positivity are excluded.
dat_pos <- surv_base %>%
  mutate(entry_age = pmax(origin_age, est_age_pos)) %>%
  filter(if_else(is.finite(R_age), R_age > entry_age, L_age > entry_age)) %>%
  mutate(L_pos = pmax(L_age - entry_age, 0),
         R_pos = R_age - entry_age)

# Sample flow and characteristics quoted in the Results
surv_summary <- with(surv_base, c(
  n = length(RID), events = sum(event), before_positivity = sum(bio_neg),
  non_ad = sum(cens_imp & !bio_neg), unimpaired = sum(!cens_imp & !event),
  median_age = median(origin_age), pct_female = 100 * mean(sex == "Female"),
  median_educ = median(edu),
  pct_apoe4 = 100 * mean(apoe %in% c("e24", "e34", "e44")),
  median_fu = visits_ptau %>% filter(RID %in% surv_base$RID) %>%
    group_by(RID) %>%
    summarize(fu = as.numeric(max(cdr_date - v0_date)) / 365.25) %>%
    pull(fu) %>% median(),
  n_timescale_b = nrow(dat_pos),
  start_at_positivity = sum(dat_pos$est_age_pos > dat_pos$origin_age)))

title: Predicting the age of Alzheimer’s symptom onset from a blood test: evaluating a prognostic claim
text:
Common-trajectory assumption
The clock assumes that individuals with the same %p-tau217 level follow the same trajectory. A single observed %p-tau217 value, the quantity available from one blood test, explained 6% of the between-person variance in the rate of change in the ADNI clock-development sample (adjusted R² 0.06, 95% CI 0.02 to 0.10; Figure 6, panel a). Substituting the model-based value at the midpoint of follow-up, which incorporates the participant’s own rate of change, raised the explained variance to 17% (adjusted R² 0.17, 95% CI 0.11 to 0.24; Figure 6, panel b).
Consider two participants, both with a %p-tau217 of 3.0, just below the positivity threshold of 4.06. The 95% prediction interval for their rates at that level runs from below zero to roughly 0.5 per year: one may cross the threshold within a couple of years, while the other may never cross it at all, yet the clock assigns them the same estimated time to positivity.
Under either definition of level, the overwhelming majority of the variance in rate is left unexplained.


Show code: common-trajectory analysis
# Points: conditional-mean (BLUP) slope per participant.
# Curve:  GAM mean rate as a function of level, averaged over resamples.
# Band:   95% prediction interval for an individual's rate at a given level.
# R2:     mean adjusted R2 across resamples with its 2.5-97.5% interval.
set.seed(20260901)
n_draws <- 2000   # resamples of the random effects
n_pool  <- 200    # resamples pooled for the quantile GAM band
k_band  <- 5

ptau_rate <- ptau_long %>% filter(RID %in% clock_dev_ids)

# Linear mixed model with random intercepts and slopes in years since the
# first in-range draw
fit_lmm <- lmer(ptau217 ~ ptau_years + (1 + ptau_years | RID), data = ptau_rate)
beta <- fixef(fit_lmm)
re   <- ranef(fit_lmm, condVar = TRUE)$RID
pv   <- attr(re, "postVar")       # conditional covariance of each (b0, b1)
ids  <- rownames(re)

# (a) observed first value; (b) model-based value at the midpoint of follow-up
ptau_first <- ptau_rate %>% group_by(RID) %>% slice(1) %>%
  { setNames(.$ptau217, .$RID) } %>% .[ids]
tmid <- tapply(ptau_rate$ptau_years, ptau_rate$RID,
  function(t) (min(t) + max(t)) / 2)[ids]
slope_blup <- beta[2] + re[, 2]
mid_blup   <- beta[1] + re[, 1] + slope_blup * tmid

# One draw of every participant's (b0, b1) from its conditional distribution
draw_once <- function() {
  b <- t(sapply(seq_along(ids), function(i)
    MASS::mvrnorm(1, mu = as.numeric(re[i, ]), Sigma = pv[, , i])))
  colnames(b) <- c("b0", "b1")
  b
}

# x_fun maps a draw to the panel's level variable; x_obs is what is plotted
build_panel <- function(x_fun, x_obs) {
  grid <- seq(min(x_obs), max(x_obs), length.out = 200)
  out <- replicate(n_draws, {
    b <- draw_once()
    slope <- beta[2] + b[, "b1"]
    x <- x_fun(b, slope)
    g <- gam(slope ~ s(x))
    c(r2 = summary(g)$r.sq, predict(g, newdata = data.frame(x = grid)))
  })
  pooled <- map_dfr(seq_len(n_pool), function(i) {
    b <- draw_once()
    slope <- beta[2] + b[, "b1"]
    tibble(x = x_fun(b, slope), slope = slope)
  })
  q025 <- qgam(slope ~ s(x, k = k_band), data = pooled, qu = 0.025)
  q975 <- qgam(slope ~ s(x, k = k_band), data = pooled, qu = 0.975)
  list(
    curve = tibble(x = grid, fit = rowMeans(out[-1, ]),
      lo = as.numeric(predict(q025, newdata = data.frame(x = grid))),
      hi = as.numeric(predict(q975, newdata = data.frame(x = grid)))),
    points = tibble(x = x_obs, slope = slope_blup),
    r2 = mean(out[1, ]), r2_ci = quantile(out[1, ], c(0.025, 0.975)))
}

title: Constrained vs unconstrained longitudinal data analysis
text:
Liang and Zeger (2000) describe a constrained longitudinal data analysis for comparing the time course of two randomized groups in which the model constains the two groups to share a common mean at baseline. Lu (2010) compared the power of this approach to a longitudinal analysis of covariance approach. We conduct a few simple simulation studies to interrogate the effect of the constraint on power to detect group differences. We do not simulate any missing data here.

    cLDA.alpha = lme(Y.null~time+time:trt, random=~1|id, data=dd1)
  )

  c(unlist(prepost),
    slopes = unlist(lapply(fits, function(fit){
      summary(fit)$tTable['time:trt', 'p-value']
    })),
    contrasts = unlist(lapply(fits[1:2], function(fit){
      pv <- try(as.numeric(contrast(fit,
        a=list(time=Time[length(Time)], trt=0),
        b=list(time=Time[length(Time)], trt=1))$Pvalue), silent = TRUE)
      if(class(pv) == 'try-error'){

          a=list(time=Time[length(Time)], trt=0),
          b=list(time=Time[length(Time)], trt=1))$Pvalue), silent = TRUE)

    }))
  )

So the t-test power is fixed at 80% (by design), the unconstrained LDA has nearly identical power to t-test; while ANCOVA and constrained LDA have similar power (always better power than t-test, but power decreases with increasing pre-post correlation). ANCOVA2 has similar power as ANCOVA1 (not surprising since no interaction between baseline outcome and group was simulated).
This confirms that the cLDA is preferred whenever we have two timepoints in a randomized study; just as ANCOVA is always preferred to t-test. Of course, cLDA has the added advantage of accommodating missing data.

title: GLS, MMRM, and Missing Data
text:
The gls routine in the nlme package is sensitive to the data order when using corCompSymm, particularly when data is missing. This is alluded to in the corCompSymm documentation. Below are some examples.


When there is no missingness, there is no problem provided the data is sorted by time:

library(nlme)
set.seed(20130506)
fm1Orth.gls <- gls( distance ~ Sex * I(age - 11), 
  Orthodont,
  correlation = corSymm(form = ~ 1 | Subject),
  weights = varIdent(form = ~ 1 | age) )
summary(fm1Orth.gls)$tTable

(Intercept)           24.9371232 0.47286660 52.736063 7.204876e-77
SexFemale             -2.2717427 0.74083959 -3.066443 2.760865e-03

SexFemale:I(age - 11) -0.3504390 0.12881040 -2.720580 7.640131e-03

fm2Orth.gls <- gls( distance ~ Sex * I(age - 11), 
  Orthodont[nrow(Orthodont):1, ], # reverse order
  correlation = corSymm(form = ~ 1 | Subject),
  weights = varIdent(form = ~ 1 | age) )
summary(fm2Orth.gls)$tTable # same as sorted

                           Value  Std.Error   t-value      p-value
(Intercept)           24.9371337 0.47286148 52.736658 7.196740e-77

  Orthodont[sample(1:nrow(Orthodont), replace = TRUE), ],
  correlation = corSymm(form = ~ 1 | Subject),
  weights = varIdent(form = ~ 1 | age) )

About
Michael Donohue is Professor of Neurology at the Keck School of Medicine and Associate Director of Biostatistics at the Epstein Family Alzheimer’s Therapeutic Research Institute (ATRI). He received his PhD in Mathematics from the University of California, San Diego. Dr. Donohue applies novel statistical methods to data from natural history studies and clinical trials to better understand the multivariate course of markers of Alzheimer’s progression, and design innovative clinical trials to prevent or slow the progression of disease. He has studied the risk of cognitive decline associated with elevated brain amyloid in cognitively normal individuals; and helped design the first intervention in asymptomatic Alzheimer’s, the Anti-Amyloid Treatment for Asymptomatic Alzheimer’s (the A4 Study; in collaboration with Eli Lilly), and its primary outcome measure, the Preclinical Alzheimer Cognitive Composite. He has been awarded grants to develop innovative statistical approaches for Alzheimer’s from the National Institute on Aging; the Alzheimer’s Association, Michael J. Fox Foundation, and W. Garfield Weston Foundation; and the Clinical and Translation Research Institute of the University of California, San Diego
